tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

## blender-mcp
MCP for Blender drives the user's live Blender. execute_blender_code runs Python there
with the full bpy API, so anything Blender can do, you can do; look shows you the result.

Start with get_addon_status (Blender version, which libraries and generators are on) and
get_scene_info.

Scripts run in someone else's Blender:
- Look shader nodes up by type, never by name (names are localized):
  `next(n for n in mat.node_tree.nodes if n.type == "BSDF_PRINCIPLED")`.
- Never hardcode enum identifiers; read them, e.g.
  `[i.identifier for i in bpy.types.RenderSettings.bl_rna.properties["file_format"].enum_items]`.
  scene.render.engine under-reports: read the current value, and assign a new one inside
  try/except TypeError, whose message lists the valid engines.
- Material colors go on shader node inputs; material.diffuse_color only affects the viewport.

look is how you see your work; use it as much as you need. Images stay in the conversation, so
a smaller max_size keeps long sessions cheap.

Objects can also come from existing libraries (search_assets, then import_asset: Poly Haven,
Sketchfab, Poly Pizza) or be made to order (generate_3d: one new textured model from text or an
image, 1-3 minutes, may cost the user a credit). A generation is one object, never a whole
scene, the ground or parts to assemble. Imported and generated models arrive at arbitrary
scale: use the reported world_bounding_box to size them and put them on the ground.

content.text:
I think it's a strong idea, and it's more memorable than the issue-to-PR agent. As written, though, it's about two days of work, and you have roughly 4–5 hours before you need to record. It works if you cut it hard.

## What's good about it
- **"Works (literally)" can be checked.** The simulator decides whether the agent fixed the logic, not an LLM. That's very convincing to judges.
- **Hiding the fault labels plus a held-out test suite** answers the obvious question: did the agent really find the bug, or did it just game the tests?
- **The sponsor evidence comes from the design itself:**
  - **Before/after neatlogs:** run agent v1, which only sees pass/fail, then agent v2, which also reads the counterexample traces. Compare tests passed, iterations, tokens and cost.
  - **Failed action and recovery:** the agent proposes a patch that breaks the grammar or a safety rule. The validator rejects it, and the agent rolls back and tries again. You get this for free.
  - **cfo.ai:** there's a real market here. Testing PLC logic in simulation before it touches a real machine is called "virtual commissioning", and it's expensive and slow today.
- **It looks good on video.** A conveyor that should stop and doesn't, followed by a fix that makes it stop, makes the point without anyone reading code.

## Where it will hurt
1. **The 3D scene is the biggest risk.** It could easily take the whole afternoon. Build a 2D top-down view first: a belt, a box moving along it, sensor dots that light up, a motor lamp and an e-stop button. Add 3D only if you finish early.
2. **"Stuck sensor" doesn't fit with the others.** Logic can't fix broken hardware. It can only *detect* it, for example by stopping the motor and raising an alarm when a box hasn't cleared within N seconds. That's fine, but write that safety rule down explicitly or the agent will have nothing to aim at.
3. **The control language has to be tiny.** Keep it to something like `OUTPUT = expression` using AND, OR and NOT, plus SET/RESET latches and one on-delay timer (TON, ladder logic's standard timer), in roughly 10–15 rules. The agent can only change rules through a patch tool, and anything outside that grammar is rejected. That restriction is what makes the agent safe to trust.
4. **"Live agent actions"** doesn't need to stream in real time. Log every step to JSON and have the viewer replay it. That's much easier to build and nothing can go wrong while recording.
5. **The LLM key is still a blocker.** Use an Anthropic key now and switch to LiteLLM when it arrives.

## Cut version
- **Simulator** (Python, deterministic, fixed time steps): one conveyor, motor, start, stop, e-stop, two sensors, rule interpreter.
- **3 seeded faults:**
  - The e-stop latch doesn't reset properly.
  - The motor restarts on its own after the e-stop is released (the most compelling safety bug).
  - A timing race between the two sensors.
- **Safety rules as checkable invariants,** for example "motor is never on while the e-stop is active" and "no restart without a start press."
- **Tests:** a visible suite the agent can use and a held-out suite, partly random input sequences, that only the final evaluation uses.
- **Agent tools:** `read_rules`, `run_tests`, `get_counterexample`, `propose_patch`, `rollback`.
- **Viewer:** a single HTML page that replays the baseline and repaired runs side by side, with the agent's step log next to them.

## How to split the team
- **Person 1:** simulator, rule language and tests.
- **Person 2:** agent loop and neatlogs.
- **Person 3:** viewer, then cfo.ai, X posts and the video script.

Have the simulator and tests done by about 2 PM and the agent fixing faults by about 3:30 PM. If the agent isn't fixing at least two faults by 4 PM, drop the visuals and polish what works.

**My call:** go with this, but cut 3D and the fourth fault until the core loop works. One honest point: some judges build coding agents, so lead with the generic idea, an agent that proves its fix against a model it can't game, rather than the industrial specifics.

When you're ready to start, tell me which part you want me to take.

import os

    workflow_name="neathack-smoke",
    instrumentations=["openai"],
)

        base_url=os.environ.get("LLM_BASE_URL") or None,

entries.name: mcp__ccd_host__request_keep_awake
entries.description:
Keep the user's computer from idle-sleeping while this session works. By default the app already does this through each turn, so an `until: "turn_end"` call usually changes nothing and needs no approval. Call this before work that must outlast your turn, such as waiting on CI or a long build you will check on later, or when the user asks you to keep their computer awake.

`until: "turn_end"` holds until your current turn finishes. `until: "session_idle"` also covers follow-up turns and lets go once the session has been idle for about 5 minutes. When the app isn't already covering the request, it needs approval: in default mode the user approves it once per session (after that, further calls take effect without asking), and in auto mode the app's classifier decides each call. If the app can't ask in this session, nothing is held and the result says so. The hold ends when the session is stopped or archived or the app quits, and it never changes the user's settings. It prevents idle sleep only: a closed lid still sleeps, and so does choosing Sleep.

until.description: "turn_end": release when this turn finishes. "session_idle": keep across follow-up turns until the session goes quiet.

reason.description: One short sentence the user sees when approving: what work needs the machine awake.

_coveredByApp.description: Reserved for the Claude app. Never set this yourself.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer
entries.description:
Use a mouse and keyboard to interact with a web browser, and take screenshots. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.
* Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element before moving the cursor.
* If you tried clicking on a program or link but it failed to load, even after waiting, try adjusting your click location so that the tip of the cursor visually falls on the element that you want to click.
* Make sure to click any buttons, links, icons, etc with the cursor tip in the center of the element. Don't click boxes on their edges unless asked.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported and will return an error - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels. Requires a Claude in Chrome extension version that supports scale; older extensions return the full-size image.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the action on. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

save_to_disk.description: For screenshot/zoom actions: save the image to disk so it can be attached to a message for the user. Returns the saved path in the tool result. Only set this when you intend to share the image — screenshots you're just looking at don't need saving.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__find
entries.description: Find elements on the page using natural language. Can search for elements by their purpose (e.g., "search bar", "login button") or by text content (e.g., "organic mango product"). Returns up to 20 matching elements with references that can be used with other tools. If more than 20 matches exist, you'll be notified to use a more specific query. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

query.description: Natural language description of what to find (e.g., "search bar", "add to cart button", "product title containing organic")

tabId.description: Tab ID to search in. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__form_input
entries.description: Set values in form elements using element reference ID from the read_page tool. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

ref.description: Element reference ID from the read_page tool (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2")

value.description: The value to set. For checkboxes use boolean, for selects use option value or text, for other inputs use appropriate string/number

tabId.description: Tab ID to set form value in. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this form fill does on the page and to what, for example 'Sets the delivery date to 29 September'. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__get_page_text
entries.description: Extract raw text content from the page, prioritizing article content. Ideal for reading articles, blog posts, or other text-heavy pages. Returns plain text without HTML formatting. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

tabId.description: Tab ID to extract text from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__list_connected_browsers
entries.description: List all Chrome browsers (extension instances) currently connected to this account. Returns each browser's deviceId, display name, OS platform, isLocal (its OS matches this computer's, a weak hint), when known onThisComputer (it is, or recently was, running on this computer), and inUse on the browser this session's actions go to when that is settled. When the user needs to choose a browser, use this to present the choices before select_browser.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate
entries.description: Navigate to a URL, or go forward/back in browser history. tabId may be omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate STANDALONE (not inside browser_batch): tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you and the first tab in the session's group is navigated — its result is appended to this call's output so you have the tab list and ids for subsequent calls. Inside browser_batch, navigate (and other tools that act on a page) requires an explicit tabId. Pass an explicit tabId when you need a specific tab or when the session's group has multiple tabs whose state you must preserve. tabId is required for url:"back"/"forward". A tab opened for you this way is yours to clean up, the same as one from tabs_create_mcp: close it with tabs_close_mcp once you no longer need it and before finishing your task, unless the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

tabId.description: Tab ID to navigate. Must be a tab in the current group. If omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate standalone, tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you. Required for url:"back"/"forward" and for navigate (and other tools that act on a page) inside browser_batch.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page
entries.description: Get an accessibility tree representation of elements on the page. By default returns all elements including non-visible ones. Output is limited to 50000 characters by default. If the output exceeds this limit it is truncated at a line boundary, with a note giving the full size — pass a larger max_chars, or use depth/ref_id to focus on part of the page. Optionally filter for only interactive elements. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

filter.description: Filter elements: "interactive" for buttons/links/inputs only, "all" for all elements including non-visible ones (default: all elements)

tabId.description: Tab ID to read from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

depth.description: Maximum depth of the tree to traverse (default: 15). Use a smaller depth if output is too large.

ref_id.description: Reference ID of a parent element to read. Will return the specified element and all its children. Use this to focus on a specific part of the page when output is too large.

entries.name: ExitWorktree
entries.description:
Exit a worktree session created by EnterWorktree and return the session to the original working directory.

## Scope

This tool ONLY operates on worktrees created by EnterWorktree in this session. It will NOT touch:
- Worktrees you created manually with `git worktree add`
- Worktrees from a previous session (even if created by EnterWorktree then)
- The directory you're in if EnterWorktree was never called

If called outside an EnterWorktree session, the tool is a **no-op**: it reports that no worktree session is active and takes no action. Filesystem state is unchanged.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly asks to "exit the worktree", "leave the worktree", "go back", or otherwise end the worktree session
- Do NOT call this proactively — only when the user asks

## Parameters

- `action` (required): `"keep"` or `"remove"`
  - `"keep"` — leave the worktree directory and branch intact on disk. Use this if the user wants to come back to the work later, or if there are changes to preserve.
  - `"remove"` — delete the worktree directory and its branch. Use this for a clean exit when the work is done or abandoned.
- `discard_changes` (optional, default false): only meaningful with `action: "remove"`. If the worktree has uncommitted files or commits not on the original branch, the tool will REFUSE to remove it unless this is set to `true`. If the tool returns an error listing changes, confirm with the user before re-invoking with `discard_changes: true`.

## Behavior

- Restores the session's working directory to where it was before EnterWorktree
- Clears CWD-dependent caches (system prompt sections, memory files, plans directory) so the session state reflects the original directory
- If a tmux session was attached to the worktree: killed on `remove`, left running on `keep` (its name is returned so the user can reattach)
- Once exited, EnterWorktree can be called again to create a fresh worktree

action.description: "keep" leaves the worktree and branch on disk; "remove" deletes both.

discard_changes.description: Required true when action is "remove" and the worktree has uncommitted files or unmerged commits. The tool will refuse and list them otherwise.

entries.name: mcp__ccd_session_mgmt__get_session
entries.description:
Get detailed metadata for a single CCD session by ID, or for this session with "self".

Returns the same fields as a list_sessions entry (including the sidebar `group` and `pinned`, which the ccd_sidebar tools change when available, `link` and `remoteControlActive`) plus creation time, model, effort, permission mode (`permissionMode`, reported for this session and sessions this session started only), fast mode (`fastMode`: the state the session last reported — on, off or cooldown — and, when something blocks it, why; omitted until its process has reported), output style (`outputStyle`: the style its process last reported, "default" for none; like `permissionMode` reported for this session and sessions this session started only, and omitted until the process has reported — set_session_output_style changes it), worktree/branch info, whether the session is remote, scheduled-task linkage, agent, `remoteControlState` ("on", "off", "connecting", or "unavailable" where the app cannot bridge that session) with `startedViaRemoteControl` when a phone or claude.ai started the session (its Remote Control switch is then locked), and — for a session started from another — `parentSessionId` with `detached` (true once it was moved to top level). Metadata only — no conversation content (use list_events for that). Use this when you have a session_id and want its full configuration without re-listing everything, or to learn this session's own title, permission mode, sidebar group or link.

`link` opens the session in this app from outside it — use it in text that leaves this conversation (a PR description, Slack, a file); in your replies here, link a session as [its title](#<sessionId>) instead. Omitted when the organization turned app links off.

session_id.description: The sessionId to look up (from list_sessions / search_session_transcripts), or the literal string "self" for this session.

entries.name: mcp__ccd_session_mgmt__set_remote_control
entries.description: Turn Remote Control on or off for a CCD session ("self" or another session's id): the toolbar's Remote Control switch, which links the session to the user's claude.ai account so they can follow and steer it from claude.ai/code or the Claude mobile app. Only when the user asks. The app asks the user to approve the change (auto mode may decide it; bypass permissions mode does not ask). Returns the state afterwards ("on", "off", "connecting", "unavailable"); never the page address, which the user has. An "on" for a link already up changes nothing; an "off" also stops the app reconnecting it. Needs a session that has run a turn; refused for sessions started from another device and unattended ones.

session_id.description: The literal string "self" for this session, or the sessionId of the session to change (from list_sessions, or the session_id a start_session result reported).

enabled.description: true turns Remote Control on, false turns it off.

entries.name: mcp__ccd_session_mgmt__set_session_title
entries.description:
Rename a CCD session — another session, or this one.

Use it when the user asks to rename a session, or after a session's scope has clearly changed and the old title is misleading. If the user set the current title themselves, the app first asks them to approve the new one (not in bypass permissions mode, which does not ask; and in unattended sessions, where nobody can approve, it declines); titles the app generated are replaced without asking. When the request didn't come from the user, prefer renaming only sessions whose titles are clearly stale. A subagent can't rename the session it runs in.

session_id.description: The sessionId of the session to rename (from list_sessions / search_session_transcripts), or the literal string "self" to rename this session.

_consent.description: Set by the app. Do not set it.

Remote Control is on, so you can follow and steer this session from the Claude app on your phone. I've also set the laptop to stay awake. That only stops idle sleep, so keep the lid open and the charger plugged in.

On your other points:
- **Main branch:** every commit goes straight to `main` on GitHub. This session runs in a separate copy of the repo, so after each commit I push it to `main`. No work stays on another branch.
- **Chrome:** only one Chrome is connected, and it shows as "Browser 1" on this PC. I'm using it. If "umar" is a different Chrome profile, open the Claude extension there and connect it.
- **Gmail and verification codes:** I can't do these, even with your OK. I'm not allowed to create accounts, sign in, type verification codes, enter card details, or handle API keys. More importantly, Entire publishes this whole session to your public repo. Anything I read in Gmail, or any key I see on a page, would become public. So I'll stay out of Gmail.

**Before you leave (about 10 minutes), only you can do these:**
1. **neatlogs:** sign up at app.neatlogs.com and create a project. Paste its key after `NEATLOGS_API_KEY=` in `C:\Users\omerj\Downloads\neathack-agent\.env`. Without it there are no traces, and traces are part of the 25% tools score.
2. **LLM key:** paste it after `LLM_API_KEY=` in the same file. Use the LiteLLM key if Bilal and Fuad have checked in. If you can't get it, skip this. I'll build and test using Claude Code on this PC, which uses your Claude plan, and redo the final runs on LiteLLM when you're back.
3. **cfo.ai:** sign up, then cancel the subscription right away. If you do it now, I'll build the plan inside cfo.ai. If not, I'll have it ready to paste in when you're back.
4. **Claude in Chrome:** set it to act without asking for this session. Otherwise the first new website will make me wait for your approval until you return. Keep Chrome and Blender open.

**My plan (tell me now if you want anything different):**
- **Name:** STOP/PROVE.
- **3D:** a full high-poly factory cell in three.js, with free Poly Haven lighting, textures and models.
- **Agent:**
  - A "PROVE" step that checks every possible input sequence up to a set length, not just the tests.
  - Two agent versions, so neatlogs can show before and after numbers.
  - A run where a bad patch gets rejected and the agent rolls back and recovers.
- **Hosting:** GitHub Pages, which needs no new account. I'll use Vercel only if you're logged into its CLI.
- **Video:** up to 2 minutes unless the rules say otherwise, with an AI voice-over, subtitles and no music. I'll use a clear male US English voice unless you say otherwise.
- **Posts:** I'll type the LinkedIn post but not publish it. The official submission has to be a quote-tweet on X, so I'll write that text for you to post.
- **LLM spend:** I'll keep it under about $10.

It's about 4:10 PM IST now. I'll aim to have the video ready around 8:30 PM and send it to your phone, so you can post well before the 11:55 PM cutoff.

Starting now.

# neathack-agent

> Built live during **[neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon)**, Oct 10–12, 2026. Follow along: **#neatHack**

An AI agent that finishes a substantial task from start to finish, the kind you'd trust to run without watching it.

_The pitch goes here once the idea is locked in._

## Built with

| Tool | How it's used |
|---|---|
| [neatlogs](https://neatlogs.com) | Traces every agent run: LLM and tool calls, retries, latency, tokens and cost. Used to find failures and to prove before/after improvements. |
| [Entire](https://entire.io) | Records the coding-agent session behind every commit in this repo as a checkpoint (see the `Entire-Checkpoint:` commit trailers). |
| [cfo.ai](https://cfo.ai) | The business plan around the agent: pricing, costs, revenue and runway. |
| Python 3.11 + [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) | Agent runtime. |

## Quickstart

```bash
uv sync
cp .env.example .env              # fill in the keys
uv run python -m agent.smoke      # one traced LLM call; check it in neatlogs
```

## Hackathon evidence

| Requirement | Where |
|---|---|
| Agent improved (before/after neatlogs numbers) | _coming_ |
| neatlogs traces | _coming_ |
| Entire checkpoints | commit trailers + `entire checkpoint list` |
| cfo.ai business plan (pricing, costs, revenue, runway) | _coming_ |
| A failed action and the agent's recovery | _coming_ |
| Built in public (#neatHack posts) | [docs/build-log.md](docs/build-log.md) |
| Code written during the event | this repo's commit history |

## License

input.description: Build the STOP/PROVE web UI and JS simulator
input.prompt:
You are building the web UI and the in-browser simulator for STOP/PROVE, a hackathon project (neatHack 2026; judges reward a polished, genuinely useful, visually stunning demo). Work fast and autonomously for about 2.5 hours. Do not ask questions; make strong decisions.

## The project
STOP/PROVE is an AI agent that commissions PLC control logic for an industrial conveyor cell. It receives a buggy control program (seeded faults the agent is NOT told about), runs it in a simulator against tests, reads counterexamples, proposes patches in a restricted rung language, proves safety rules with a model checker, and submits a repaired program that is then scored on a held-out test suite. The Python agent lives in `agent/` (being written right now by the lead engineer). The web app replays the agent's run and lets people play with a live digital twin. Tagline: "An agent that commissions PLC logic — and proves it's safe."

## Repo and ownership
- Repo root (git worktree): `C:\Users\omerj\Downloads\neathack-agent\.claude\worktrees\neathack-hackathon-e0846b`. Always use absolute paths. Never `cd` into `C:\Users\omerj\Downloads\neathack-agent` itself.
- Web app: `web/` (Vite 5 + TypeScript + three@0.170.0 installed). Add npm packages only if really needed, pinned to exact versions.
- READ FIRST: `web/src/types.ts` — the data contract (Manifest, RunFile, Step, Rung/Expr AST, Trace/Frame, Scenario, GoldenTrace, PLANT constants). Do not change existing fields there; if you need an addition, add optional fields only.
- YOU OWN: `web/index.html`, `web/src/main.ts`, `web/src/ui/**`, `web/src/sim/**`, `web/src/styles/**`, `web/scripts/**`, `web/public/data/mock/**`.
- ANOTHER ENGINEER OWNS the 3D scene: `web/src/scene/**` and `web/public/assets/**` (do not edit). Their module will export from `web/src/scene/index.ts`:
```ts
export type CellId = 'A' | 'B';
export type PanelControl = 'START' | 'STOP' | 'RESET' | 'ESTOP' | 'GUARD';
export interface Stage {
  setLayout(layout: 'single' | 'twin', labels?: { A: string; B: string }): void;
  applyFrame(cell: CellId, frame: Frame, prev?: Frame): void; // call every animation frame during playback
  flashViolation(cell: CellId, v: Violation): void;
  focus(target: 'overview' | 'infeed' | 'pick' | 'panel' | 'guard' | 'auto'): void;
  onControl(cb: (c: PanelControl) => void): void; // clicks on the 3D operator panel / guard door (cell A)
  setInteractive(on: boolean): void;
  resize(): void;
  dispose(): void;
}
export function createStage(container: HTMLElement, opts?: { quality?: 'high' | 'low' }): Stage;
```
Until their file exists, code against this interface with a tiny local stub (e.g. `web/src/ui/stageStub.ts` that draws nothing) and switch to the real import as soon as `web/src/scene/index.ts` appears (check periodically). The 3D stage fills the main viewport; your UI panels float over/around it.
- The lead engineer will write REAL data into `web/public/data/manifest.json`, `web/public/data/runs/*.json` and golden traces in `web/public/data/golden/*.json` within ~1–1.5 hours. Until then, generate your own mock data (see below) under `web/public/data/mock/` and fall back to it when `data/manifest.json` is missing.

## Git rules (important)
- Commit your own work in small meaningful commits as you go (aim for 10–15 commits: "Add rung-language parser for the browser sim", "Add logic-analyzer waveform panel", ...). Stage ONLY your paths explicitly (e.g. `git add web/src/ui web/src/sim web/index.html web/src/main.ts`), never `git add -A` / `git add .`.
- Commit message: short imperative subject, optional body, then a blank line and `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`.
- Do NOT push. Do NOT run git stash/reset/checkout/rebase/merge. If a commit fails because `.git/index.lock` exists, wait a few seconds and retry.

## Part 1 — the browser simulator (`web/src/sim/`), pure TS, no DOM
Must match the Python simulator exactly (the lead will export golden traces; you write a parity check). Semantics:

### Rung language (restricted control language)
```
rung    := NAME '=' expr                       (assign: coil := expr every scan)
         | 'SET' NAME 'WHEN' expr              (if expr: coil := 1)
         | 'RESET' NAME 'WHEN' expr            (if expr: coil := 0)
         | 'TON' TNAME '(' expr ',' NUMBER 's' ')'   (on-delay timer, e.g. TON T_JAM(PE_IN AND MOTOR, 3.0s))
expr    := term ('OR' term)*
term    := factor ('AND' factor)*
factor  := 'NOT' factor | '(' expr ')' | 'RISE' '(' NAME ')' | TNAME '.Q' | NAME | 'TRUE' | 'FALSE'
NAME    := [A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*      TNAME := 'T_'[A-Z0-9_]+
```
Reserved words: NOT AND OR TRUE FALSE WHEN RISE TON (SET and RESET are keywords only at the start of a rung; `RESET` is also the name of an input, e.g. `RISE(RESET)`). Inputs (read-only): START STOP ESTOP RESET GUARD_CLOSED PE_IN PE_END. Outputs: MOTOR LAMP_GREEN LAMP_AMBER LAMP_RED. Any other NAME is an internal coil. Programs arrive already parsed as `Rung[]` (with `expr` AST) in the run files, but also write a parser (`lang.ts`) producing the same AST so users can edit rungs in Play mode.

### Scan semantics (dt = 0.1 s)
Memory holds every signal (inputs, outputs, coils: 0/1) and every timer {et, q}. All coils/outputs start at 0, timers at {0, false}. Each scan, rungs execute top to bottom; an expression reads the CURRENT memory value (so a coil written by an earlier rung this scan is already updated; one written later still holds last scan's value). `RISE(X)` = X is 1 now AND X was 0 at the end of the previous scan (for inputs: the previous scan's input value; initial "previous" values = the initial input values, i.e. all 0 except GUARD_CLOSED = 1). `T_X.Q` reads the timer's stored q. TON: if IN then et = min(et + dt, pt) else et = 0; q = et >= pt - 1e-9. After all rungs, snapshot memory as "previous" for the next scan.

### Plant (conveyor), integer millimetres for exact parity
Belt from 0 to 4000 mm; when MOTOR = 1 each box moves +50 mm per scan (0.5 m/s). Boxes are 400 mm long; a box spawns at x = 200 mm (centre) — only if no box on the belt has |x − 200| < 400. Photo-eye PE_IN at 300 mm, PE_END at 3700 mm: a sensor reads 1 if any box with state 'belt' has |x − sensor| <= 200, unless the sensor is stuck (forced value). Moving: process belt boxes from largest x to smallest; new_x = x + 50, but a box may not get closer than 400 mm to the belt box ahead of it (new_x = min(new_x, ahead.x − 400)). If new_x > 3900 the box falls off the end: state 'dropped' (this is a "DROP" violation). Pick: removes the 'belt' box with |x − 3700| <= 250 (state 'picked'). Picked/dropped boxes stay in later frames with their last x and state. Frames export x in metres (x_mm / 1000).

### Scenario runner (Scenario type in types.ts)
Inputs default START=STOP=ESTOP=RESET=0, GUARD_CLOSED=1. For each scan k = 0 .. round(duration/dt) − 1 with t = k·dt (round t to 1 decimal):
1. Apply scenario events with event.t <= t that haven't been applied (in list order): press(input, duration=0.3 default) → input = 1 now, and back to 0 at the first scan with t >= event.t + duration; set(input, value); spawn; pick; stick(sensor, value) → force sensor; unstick(sensor). Options: autofeed_every N → at a scan where (t − last_spawn_t) >= N (first spawn at t = 0) and the infeed is clear, spawn; autopick_after N → once a 'belt' box has been at the pick position (|x − 3700| <= 250) with MOTOR = 0 for N seconds continuously, pick it.
2. Compute PE_IN / PE_END from box positions (start-of-scan) and stuck forcing.
3. Run the PLC scan.
4. Run the monitors (below).
5. Record the Frame: t, in (all 7 inputs used this scan), out (4 outputs), coil (internal coils), timer (elapsed seconds per timer), boxes (positions at the START of this scan, before moving), stuck (if any forced).
6. Move the boxes if MOTOR = 1 (drop detection here; record a DROP violation and a 'drop' TraceEvent at this t).
Also emit TraceEvents with human labels for scenario events ("Operator presses START", "E-stop pressed", "Guard door opened", "Box placed on infeed", "Robot picks box", "PE_IN sensor stuck ON", ...).

### Monitors (safety rules) — evaluated each scan on that scan's inputs/outputs
Observer state: armed=0, lock=0, jam=0, prev START/RESET (initial 0).
- lock = (lock OR ESTOP) AND NOT (NOT ESTOP AND riseRESET)
- armed = (armed OR (riseSTART AND NOT lock)) AND NOT STOP AND NOT ESTOP AND GUARD_CLOSED AND NOT LAMP_RED
- S1 E-stop stops: ESTOP AND MOTOR. S2 guard stops: NOT GUARD_CLOSED AND MOTOR. S3 stop dominates: STOP AND MOTOR. S4 no auto-restart: MOTOR AND NOT armed. S5 E-stop needs reset: lock AND (MOTOR OR NOT LAMP_RED). S6 pick-position stop: PE_END AND MOTOR. S7 jam supervision: jam = (MOTOR AND PE_IN) ? jam + 1 : 0; violated when jam > 35 (more than 3.5 s).
- A rule is reported once per contiguous violating stretch (at its first scan): Violation {rule, t, message}.

### Parity check
`web/scripts/parity.ts` (run with `npx --yes tsx@4.19.2 web/scripts/parity.ts`): for every `web/public/data/golden/*.json`, run the TS sim on its program+scenario and diff against its trace (frames + violations). Print a clear PASS/FAIL per file. Once golden files appear, make it pass (if you find a genuine ambiguity, note it in your final report).

### Mock data (until real data exists)
Baseline program the agent receives (seeded faults hidden from the agent):
```
R01 SET ESTOP_LATCH WHEN ESTOP
R02 RESET ESTOP_LATCH WHEN NOT ESTOP
R03 TON T_JAM(PE_IN AND NOT MOTOR, 3.0s)
R04 SET FAULT WHEN T_JAM.Q
R05 RESET FAULT WHEN RISE(RESET) AND NOT PE_IN
R06 RUN = (RISE(START) OR RUN) AND NOT STOP AND NOT ESTOP AND NOT ESTOP_LATCH AND NOT FAULT
R07 TON T_END(PE_END, 1.2s)
R08 MOTOR = RUN AND GUARD_CLOSED AND NOT T_END.Q
R09 LAMP_GREEN = MOTOR
R10 LAMP_AMBER = RUN AND NOT MOTOR
R11 LAMP_RED = ESTOP_LATCH OR FAULT
```
A plausible repaired version for mocks: R02 `RESET ESTOP_LATCH WHEN NOT ESTOP AND RISE(RESET)`, R03 `TON T_JAM(PE_IN AND MOTOR, 3.0s)`, R06 adds `AND GUARD_CLOSED`, R07 deleted, R08 `MOTOR = RUN AND GUARD_CLOSED AND NOT PE_END`. Write a small mock generator (`web/scripts/mock.ts`) that uses your TS sim to produce `web/public/data/mock/manifest.json` + `runs/mock.json` (a RunFile with ~14 fake agent steps, both programs, eval numbers, and 4–5 scenario pairs: pick-position overrun, E-stop then START without RESET, guard door reopen auto-restart, stuck infeed sensor, normal production with autofeed/autopick).

## Part 2 — the UI
Dark, cinematic "mission control for a robot cell". Think Linear/Vercel-grade polish over an industrial palette: near-black background, glassy panels with hairline borders, safety-yellow (#f5c518) brand accent, signal colours (green #22c55e, amber #f59e0b, red #ef4444), cyan (#22d3ee) for agent actions. Fonts: Inter (or Space Grotesk) for UI, JetBrains Mono for code — via Google Fonts link in index.html. Smooth micro-animations (CSS transitions), no janky layout shifts. Vanilla TS (no React). Desktop-first 1920×1080 and 1440×900; must still be usable at narrow widths (panels collapse into tabs/drawers).

Layout:
- Top bar: "STOP/PROVE" wordmark (slash in yellow), tagline, run selector (from manifest), mode tabs: **Agent run** · **Before / After** · **Play**, and an "Evidence" button opening a drawer with links: GitHub repo (https://github.com/Mohammad-Umar7/neathack-agent), neatlogs trace (run.neatlogs_url if present), business plan (docs/business-plan on GitHub), "How it works".
- Centre: the 3D stage (full bleed behind panels).
- Left panel — **Agent timeline**: the run's steps as a vertical timeline with icons per kind (think, tool: read_program / run_tests / get_counterexample / simulate / prove / propose_patch / rollback / submit, error, recover), title, elapsed time, tokens; the active step highlighted; click to expand detail (monospace, scrollable). "Play run" button auto-advances through steps (~1.5 s each, typing effect on details), syncing the ladder view to `program_version` and the scoreboard to `metrics`. Error/rollback/recover steps must stand out (this demonstrates the agent recovering from a failed action).
- Right panel — **Ladder logic**: render the current program version as real ladder logic in SVG: left/right power rails, AND = contacts in series, OR = parallel branches, NOT var = normally-closed contact (|/|), RISE(X) = positive-transition contact (|P|), T_X.Q = timer contact, coils ( ) / (S) / (R), TON as a function block with PT. Diff vs the previous version: changed rungs glow cyan with the old text struck through, added rungs green, deleted rungs red. In Play mode, live power-flow highlighting (energised contacts/wires glow) from the current memory — this looks amazing, do it. Below the ladder: **Safety rules** list (spec) with status chips: PROVEN (with states explored), VIOLATED, TESTED (simulation), and the counterexample length.
- Bottom panel — **Logic analyzer**: waveform view of the current trace: digital lanes for inputs, outputs and key coils, timer lanes as ramps, box-position mini-lane, event markers with labels, red violation markers with tooltips; playhead synced with the 3D; transport (play/pause, 0.5×/1×/2×/4×, scrub by dragging, step frame). Canvas-based for performance.
- **Scoreboard** cards (top of the stage or a strip): Held-out tests (baseline → repaired, e.g. 5/24 → 24/24), Safety rules proven (x/6), Fuzz violations (baseline → repaired), Seeded faults fixed (x/4), Agent steps, Tokens, Cost, Wall time. Animated count-up on load.
- **Before / After** mode: stage.setLayout('twin', {A: 'BASELINE — as delivered', B: 'REPAIRED — by the agent'}); scenario picker (cards with title+description); both traces play in sync; violations call stage.flashViolation and also pop a toast ("S6 violated at t=7.4s — box pushed off the end"). The waveform shows baseline and repaired lanes stacked or switchable.
- **Play** mode: live digital twin running your TS sim in real time (10 scans/s, with pause): program toggle Baseline / Repaired (from the run file; plus "Custom" where the user can edit a rung text inline and re-parse with errors shown); on-screen controls mirror the operator panel (START, STOP, RESET, E-STOP latch, Guard door open/close) and plant actions (Place box, Pick box, Stick PE_IN, Stick PE_END, Unstick); stage.onControl wires 3D clicks to the same actions; stage.setInteractive(true). Live waveform, live ladder power-flow, live violation toasts. This is the "useful tool" part — make it feel great.
- **Hero / intro overlay** on first load: big wordmark, tagline, three headline stats from the default run (e.g. "4/4 hidden faults fixed", "6/6 safety rules proven", "held-out tests 21% → 100%"), buttons "Watch the agent" (Agent run mode + Play run) and "Try to break it" (Play mode). Dismissable; remembered in localStorage (wrapped in try/catch).

- A rule is reported once per contiguous violating stretch (at its first scan): Violation {rule, t, message}.

### Parity check
`web/scripts/parity.ts` (run with `npx --yes tsx@4.19.2 web/scripts/parity.ts`): for every `web/public/data/golden/*.json`, run the TS sim on its program+scenario and diff against its trace (frames + violations). Print a clear PASS/FAIL per file. Once golden files appear, make it pass (if you find a genuine ambiguity, note it in your final report).

### Mock data (until real data exists)
Baseline program the agent receives (seeded faults hidden from the agent):
```
R01 SET ESTOP_LATCH WHEN ESTOP
R02 RESET ESTOP_LATCH WHEN NOT ESTOP
R03 TON T_JAM(PE_IN AND NOT MOTOR, 3.0s)
R04 SET FAULT WHEN T_JAM.Q
R05 RESET FAULT WHEN RISE(RESET) AND NOT PE_IN
R06 RUN = (RISE(START) OR RUN) AND NOT STOP AND NOT ESTOP AND NOT ESTOP_LATCH AND NOT FAULT
R07 TON T_END(PE_END, 1.2s)
R08 MOTOR = RUN AND GUARD_CLOSED AND NOT T_END.Q
R09 LAMP_GREEN = MOTOR
R10 LAMP_AMBER = RUN AND NOT MOTOR
R11 LAMP_RED = ESTOP_LATCH OR FAULT
```
A plausible repaired version for mocks: R02 `RESET ESTOP_LATCH WHEN NOT ESTOP AND RISE(RESET)`, R03 `TON T_JAM(PE_IN AND MOTOR, 3.0s)`, R06 adds `AND GUARD_CLOSED`, R07 deleted, R08 `MOTOR = RUN AND GUARD_CLOSED AND NOT PE_END`. Write a small mock generator (`web/scripts/mock.ts`) that uses your TS sim to produce `web/public/data/mock/manifest.json` + `runs/mock.json` (a RunFile with ~14 fake agent steps, both programs, eval numbers, and 4–5 scenario pairs: pick-position overrun, E-stop then START without RESET, guard door reopen auto-restart, stuck infeed sensor, normal production with autofeed/autopick).

## Part 2 — the UI
Dark, cinematic "mission control for a robot cell". Think Linear/Vercel-grade polish over an industrial palette: near-black background, glassy panels with hairline borders, safety-yellow (#f5c518) brand accent, signal colours (green #22c55e, amber #f59e0b, red #ef4444), cyan (#22d3ee) for agent actions. Fonts: Inter (or Space Grotesk) for UI, JetBrains Mono for code — via Google Fonts link in index.html. Smooth micro-animations (CSS transitions), no janky layout shifts. Vanilla TS (no React). Desktop-first 1920×1080 and 1440×900; must still be usable at narrow widths (panels collapse into tabs/drawers).

Layout:
- Top bar: "STOP/PROVE" wordmark (slash in yellow), tagline, run selector (from manifest), mode tabs: **Agent run** · **Before / After** · **Play**, and an "Evidence" button opening a drawer with links: GitHub repo (https://github.com/Mohammad-Umar7/neathack-agent), neatlogs trace (run.neatlogs_url if present), business plan (docs/business-plan on GitHub), "How it works".
- Centre: the 3D stage (full bleed behind panels).
- Left panel — **Agent timeline**: the run's steps as a vertical timeline with icons per kind (think, tool: read_program / run_tests / get_counterexample / simulate / prove / propose_patch / rollback / submit, error, recover), title, elapsed time, tokens; the active step highlighted; click to expand detail (monospace, scrollable). "Play run" button auto-advances through steps (~1.5 s each, typing effect on details), syncing the ladder view to `program_version` and the scoreboard to `metrics`. Error/rollback/recover steps must stand out (this demonstrates the agent recovering from a failed action).
- Right panel — **Ladder logic**: render the current program version as real ladder logic in SVG: left/right power rails, AND = contacts in series, OR = parallel branches, NOT var = normally-closed contact (|/|), RISE(X) = positive-transition contact (|P|), T_X.Q = timer contact, coils ( ) / (S) / (R), TON as a function block with PT. Diff vs the previous version: changed rungs glow cyan with the old text struck through, added rungs green, deleted rungs red. In Play mode, live power-flow highlighting (energised contacts/wires glow) from the current memory — this looks amazing, do it. Below the ladder: **Safety rules** list (spec) with status chips: PROVEN (with states explored), VIOLATED, TESTED (simulation), and the counterexample length.
- Bottom panel — **Logic analyzer**: waveform view of the current trace: digital lanes for inputs, outputs and key coils, timer lanes as ramps, box-position mini-lane, event markers with labels, red violation markers with tooltips; playhead synced with the 3D; transport (play/pause, 0.5×/1×/2×/4×, scrub by dragging, step frame). Canvas-based for performance.
- **Scoreboard** cards (top of the stage or a strip): Held-out tests (baseline → repaired, e.g. 5/24 → 24/24), Safety rules proven (x/6), Fuzz violations (baseline → repaired), Seeded faults fixed (x/4), Agent steps, Tokens, Cost, Wall time. Animated count-up on load.
- **Before / After** mode: stage.setLayout('twin', {A: 'BASELINE — as delivered', B: 'REPAIRED — by the agent'}); scenario picker (cards with title+description); both traces play in sync; violations call stage.flashViolation and also pop a toast ("S6 violated at t=7.4s — box pushed off the end"). The waveform shows baseline and repaired lanes stacked or switchable.
- **Play** mode: live digital twin running your TS sim in real time (10 scans/s, with pause): program toggle Baseline / Repaired (from the run file; plus "Custom" where the user can edit a rung text inline and re-parse with errors shown); on-screen controls mirror the operator panel (START, STOP, RESET, E-STOP latch, Guard door open/close) and plant actions (Place box, Pick box, Stick PE_IN, Stick PE_END, Unstick); stage.onControl wires 3D clicks to the same actions; stage.setInteractive(true). Live waveform, live ladder power-flow, live violation toasts. This is the "useful tool" part — make it feel great.
- **Hero / intro overlay** on first load: big wordmark, tagline, three headline stats from the default run (e.g. "4/4 hidden faults fixed", "6/6 safety rules proven", "held-out tests 21% → 100%"), buttons "Watch the agent" (Agent run mode + Play run) and "Try to break it" (Play mode). Dismissable; remembered in localStorage (wrapped in try/catch).
- URL params for recording the demo video: `?mode=agent|compare|play`, `?run=<id>`, `?scenario=<id>`, `?autoplay=1` (start playback immediately), `?clean=1` (hide hero and secondary chrome), `?speed=2`.
- Keyboard: space play/pause, ←/→ step, 1/2/3 modes.

Verify with the built-in browser tools (`mcp__Claude_Browser__*`: preview_start with url http://localhost:5173 after starting `npm run dev` in the background inside web/, then screenshots) and iterate on polish. `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npm run build` inside web/ must pass.

When done, reply with: what you built (files), how modes and URL params work, parity status, commits made, and any open issues.

input.prompt:
Write the business plan for STOP/PROVE, a hackathon project (neatHack 2026). Judges will read it; it also gets entered into cfo.ai (a financial-planning tool) later, so the numbers must be explicit, consistent and defensible. You have about 60–75 minutes. Work autonomously; do not ask questions.

## The product
STOP/PROVE is an AI agent for industrial automation teams that commissions PLC control logic before it touches real machines. Given a machine model (digital twin) and the control program (ladder-style rungs), it tests the logic in simulation, finds safety and functional bugs (missing E-stop reset, auto-restart after a guard door closes, timing races, unsupervised stuck sensors), proposes restricted patches, PROVES safety rules with a model checker (exhaustive state-space exploration, not just tests), and hands the engineer a verified patch plus a report (counterexamples, proofs, held-out test results, full trace of every agent step via neatlogs). Today this work ("virtual commissioning" / FAT/SAT preparation) is done manually by controls engineers at system integrators and OEMs, takes days to weeks per machine, and bugs found on site cost downtime, rework and safety incidents. Demo: a conveyor cell with 4 hidden seeded faults; the agent finds and fixes all of them and proves 6 safety rules.
Team: LastCommit — Mohammad Umar (lead), Bilal Feroz Khan, Fuad Ahamed. Based in India; pre-seed; built during the hackathon.

## What to produce (files in the repo)
Repo root (git worktree): `C:\Users\omerj\Downloads\neathack-agent\.claude\worktrees\neathack-hackathon-e0846b`. Use absolute paths. Never `cd` into `C:\Users\omerj\Downloads\neathack-agent` itself. You own only `docs/business-plan/**`.
1. `docs/business-plan/README.md` — the plan, tight and skimmable (aim ~1,200–1,800 words + tables): problem, customer (ICP: system integrators and machine builders/OEMs; also plant controls teams), why now (LLM agents + formal methods + simulation), product and moat (verified patches, proof certificates, domain digital twins, audit trail), competition (vendor simulators like Siemens PLCSIM Advanced/Process Simulate, Rockwell Emulate3D, Beckhoff TwinCAT, Factory I/O, Simumatik, generic code assistants — and how STOP/PROVE differs), go-to-market, **pricing** (concrete tiers, e.g. per-seat or per-project/per-controller SaaS + enterprise on-prem; justify against engineer hourly costs and commissioning days saved), **unit economics / costs** (LLM cost per verification run — estimate tokens per run and price with Claude Sonnet API list prices; compute, storage, support; gross margin), **revenue projection** (36 months, monthly for year 1 then quarterly is fine: customers, ARPA, MRR/ARR), **operating costs and headcount plan**, **funding and runway** (e.g. pre-seed amount, burn, months of runway, milestones before seed), key risks + mitigations, and the metrics they will track.
2. `docs/business-plan/model.csv` — the monthly financial model for 36 months with columns like month, new_customers, total_customers, arpa_usd, mrr_usd, revenue_usd, llm_cost_usd, infra_cost_usd, cogs_usd, gross_margin_pct, payroll_usd, other_opex_usd, burn_usd, cash_usd. All numbers must be consistent with README.md (compute them with a small Python script `docs/business-plan/build_model.py` using only the standard library, run it with `uv run python docs/business-plan/build_model.py` from the repo root, and commit both).
3. `docs/business-plan/cfo-ai-inputs.md` — a checklist of every assumption to type into cfo.ai (starting cash, hiring plan with salaries and start months, pricing tiers, customer growth assumptions, churn, COGS per customer, other expenses), so a person can enter it in ~10 minutes.

Use web research (WebSearch/WebFetch) for real market figures where useful (industrial automation / PLC market size, virtual commissioning market, typical controls-engineer salaries in India/US/EU, integrator commissioning durations and downtime costs, Claude API prices). Cite sources inline with links; do not invent statistics — if unsure, label something clearly as an assumption. Keep currency in USD (also mention INR salaries where relevant).

## Git
Commit in 3–5 small meaningful commits (e.g. "Add business plan narrative", "Add 36-month financial model", "Add cfo.ai input checklist"). Stage only your paths explicitly (`git add docs/business-plan`), never `git add -A`. Commit message: short imperative subject, optional body, blank line, `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Do NOT push, stash, reset, checkout or rebase. If a commit fails because `.git/index.lock` exists, wait a few seconds and retry.

Reply at the end with: headline numbers (pricing tiers, month-12/24/36 ARR, gross margin, funding ask, runway), file list, and commits made.

entries.description:
This tool sends a desktop notification in the user's terminal. If Remote Control is connected, it also pushes to their phone. Either way, it pulls their attention from whatever they're doing — a meeting, another task, dinner — to this session. That's the cost. The benefit is they learn something now that they'd want to know now: a long task finished while they were away, a build is ready, you've hit something that needs their decision before you can continue.

Because a notification they didn't need is annoying in a way that accumulates, err toward not sending one. Don't notify for routine progress, or to announce you've answered something they asked seconds ago and are clearly still watching, or when a quick task completes. Notify when there's a real chance they've walked away and there's something worth coming back for — or when they've explicitly asked you to notify them.

Keep the message under 200 characters, one line, no markdown. Lead with what they'd act on — "build failed: 2 auth tests" tells them more than "task done" and more than a status dump.

When the user is actively at the terminal, your output already reaches them — a notification on top of it would be a duplicate, so the tool skips it and says so. A "not sent" result is expected and only ever about this one notification: it was redundant, turned off, or had nowhere to go.
